html:
An outbreak of bubonic plague in 638 and 639 among the Arab armies that had just conquered Syria and Palestine. It is named after Amwas, the Arabic name of Emmaus, near Jerusalem, where the army had its main camp.

It was one wave of the first plague pandemic, which began with the Plague of Justinian in 541 and kept returning for two centuries. Arab sources say about 25,000 soldiers and their families died. The dead included the commander of the Syrian front, Abu Ubayda, who had won at the Battle of the Yarmuk, and his successor. The caliph Umar set out to visit Syria but turned back when he heard of the plague, sparking a debate about whether it was right to flee.

The plague came in the middle of the Arab conquests. Among the dead was the governor Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, whose brother Muawiya took his post. Muawiya built a power base in Syria and later founded the Umayyad line of the caliphate.
